solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Drunk as McGinty, frequenting bars?

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so the letters reel out of order

explanation.surface: A certain McGinty is a regular in the pubs and permanently the worse for wear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk as' looks like the start of a simile and 'bars' like pubs; the bars are the parallel and horizontal ones in a gym. The question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a pun: gymnasts work on parallel and horizontal bars, so a gymnastic person haunts bars of a non-drinking kind.

clue.text: Unfortunately, morgues are ultimately — this?

indicators.note: things that go unluckily wrong end up in a mess, so the letters are jumbled
'ultimately' means in the end, so only the word's end, its final letter, is used

explanation.surface: A rueful remark that mortuaries are, in the end, a grim sort of place.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: read straight, it asks what morgues are, and the dash stands for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An &lit: read as a sentence, the clue asks what morgues ultimately are, and places full of corpses are grisly and horrible.

clue.text: What family does at funeral with second container for ashes

parts.note: a mo = a moment, a second

explanation.surface: The mourners at a cremation wait a moment for the urn.
explanation.walkthrough: Everything in the clue belongs to the funeral, so 'second' reads as the order of events; it is MO, a brief moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the verb for the grieving that relatives do for the dead.

clue.text: Perception of a conflict with English over loch

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'over' means on top of, so one piece sits above the next

parts.note: Loch Ness, the Scottish lake of monster fame

explanation.surface: How people see a war in which the English have the upper hand over a Scottish loch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' puts E above NESS in this down entry. 'Of' just joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean the state of noticing or knowing about something.

clue.text: Composer wanting end mostly minor

indicators.note: 'mostly' means most but not all of it, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a tip is an end, as of a finger

explanation.surface: A composer who would rather avoid finishing in a minor key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minor' pretends to be a musical key beside 'Composer'; it means petty.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Sir Michael Tippett was a 20th-century English composer of operas and oratorios.

clue.text: Serious defeat embraced by Conservative, one in the soup?

indicators.note: something embraced is held in another's arms, so the first piece sits inside the second

parts.note: CON, the short form of Conservative
a rout is a crushing defeat

explanation.surface: A Tory who has presided over a crushing loss is really in the soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the soup' is an idiom for being in trouble, which fits a beaten politician; here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a crouton is a cube of fried bread floated in soup, and the question mark admits it is one of many things there.

clue.text: Man seizing power in country

indicators.note: to seize is to grab and hold, so the man holds the letter inside him

explanation.surface: A strongman takes control in a coup.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a coup; 'Man' is simply a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Himalayan kingdom, now republic, between India and China.

clue.text: Larva, one a lizard periodically rejected

indicators.note: 'periodically' means at regular intervals, so every other letter is thrown away

parts.note: ONEALIZARD with the 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th and 9th letters dropped: oNeAlIzArD

explanation.surface: A zoologist sorting specimens throws out a larva and a lizard at intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the odd letters of 'one a lizard' and the even ones remain. The word is better known as a water nymph, which is why the larval sense surprises.
explanation.definitionFit: A zoologist's sense: the aquatic young of dragonflies and mayflies are called naiads.

clue.text: What could attract a greater number to get back in ring

indicators.note: going back means running in the opposite direction, so the word turns round
'in' puts that reversed word inside the next piece

explanation.surface: A promoter wonders what would draw bigger crowds back to the boxing ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The ring looks like a boxing venue and 'a greater number' like attendance; the ring is a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a chemical released by an animal to attract a mate is the textbook example.

clue.text: Fat English king makes room for food

explanation.surface: A portly English monarch, Henry VIII perhaps, needs a whole room for his food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat' reads as describing the king; it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a cool storeroom or pantry where food is kept.

clue.text: What's seen regularly in guava, ugli — as fleshy part

indicators.note: 'regularly' means at fixed intervals, so take every other letter of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A fruit lover notices a pattern in the flesh of a guava and an ugli fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The fruits make 'fleshy part' look like pulp; it is anatomy. An ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit. The 'as' counts in the letter run.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the small fleshy lobe hanging at the back of the soft palate.

clue.text: Professional attack — always make a quick killing

parts.note: a fit is an attack, as of coughing
e'er, the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A professional assassin's creed: strike hard, and always kill fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attack' and 'killing' paint a hitman; the attack is a bout of illness, and the killing is financial.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: a 'killing' is a big profit, and to profiteer is to grab excessive gains fast, often in a crisis.

clue.text: Genuine error that's serious by reported visionary

parts.note: a sin is a grave moral error

indicators.note: a report is what is said, not written, so the word goes by its sound

parts.note: a seer is a visionary; CERE is said the same way

explanation.surface: A prophet's authentic mistake turns out to be a grave one.
explanation.walkthrough: CERE is a real word (the waxy patch on a bird's beak), but the clue only needs its sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe feelings that are real rather than put on.

clue.text: Little Jeremy Fisher story about day pond half disappeared

indicators.note: if half of it has gone, only half the word remains
'about' means around, so the story goes round the rest

parts.note: POND with half its letters gone

explanation.surface: A Beatrix Potter tale in which the frog's pond half vanishes one day.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Jeremy Fisher is the frog in Beatrix Potter's children's story, so a little one is a young frog.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a young frog, and Jeremy Fisher is literature's best-known frog, so 'little Jeremy Fisher' is one before it grows legs.

clue.text: Requiem and what it follows that might do for us?

parts.note: a requiem is a Mass for the dead
a requiem comes after a death, the snuffing out of a life

explanation.surface: A gloomy thought: a funeral service, and the death it marks, may one day be ours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do for' is British slang for kill or finish off, so the definition is a catastrophe that could wipe out humanity.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: an event wiping out a large share of species, which could include our own.

clue.text: It left a chap cold coming to a Spanish city

explanation.surface: Sex appeal abandoned a man, who was left feeling chilly on arrival in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' as sex appeal comes from the 1920s film 'It' starring Clara Bow. 'Left' reads as a verb but is just the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Salamanca is an old university city in western Spain.

clue.text: What's blue and quite sour when cooked

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so the letters are remade in a new order

explanation.surface: A riddle about some mouldy food that is blue and turns sour on cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests blue cheese or off food; the blue is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a greenish-blue shade, named after the gemstone.

clue.text: Vital I connect in conjunction

indicators.note: 'in' places the first pieces inside the last

parts.note: to mate is to join or couple

explanation.surface: It is essential that I make contact at the same time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In conjunction' reads as 'together'; conjunction is the grammatical term, standing for an example of one.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense 'full of life': a vital, lively person is animated.

clue.text: Features editor in press running after latest in pictures

indicators.note: 'in' puts the word inside the next one
'after' means following, so these pieces come behind the first

parts.note: to press someone is to urge them

explanation.surface: A newspaper's features editor, working on the press run, chases the latest pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: The newsroom surface hides a surgeon. The wordplay reads from the end of the clue backwards: the pictures piece comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic reading: features are parts of the face, and a plastic surgeon reshapes, or edits, them.

clue.text: Resigns after disturbing admission

indicators.note: to disturb is to knock out of place, so the letters are shifted

explanation.surface: An official steps down after a shocking confession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admission' in the surface is a confession; the definition means entry. 'Disturbing' reads as shocking.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal synonym: admission as the act or right of entering a place.

clue.text: Problem with a carrier missing out the last island

indicators.note: the word misses its last letter, so drop it

parts.note: a sum is an arithmetic problem
TRAM, a carrier of passengers, loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A shipping firm has trouble with a vessel that skipped the final island stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carrier' suggests a ship or airline; it is a tram.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the large Indonesian island west of Java.

clue.text: Disorganised mob, one involved in demonstration?

definitions.meaning: British slang for a useless, shambolic bunch of people
a person who demonstrates, or shows, something

explanation.surface: A chaotic crowd with a protester among them.
explanation.walkthrough: The demonstration looks like a protest march; it is a showing, and the SHOWER is the person doing it, said to rhyme with 'goer'. 'What a shower!' is a British put-down for a hopeless lot.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: British slang for a rabble, and, read as show-er, someone who shows or demonstrates.

clue.text: Hat that's key for Oscar in city

indicators.note: 'for' means in place of, so one letter stands in for another

parts.note: a homburg is a felt hat with a dented crown
A, a musical key, replaces O (Oscar in the NATO alphabet)

explanation.surface: A hat that is the key to Oscar success in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oscar looks like the film award; it is a letter in the phonetic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the major German port on the Elbe.

clue.text: Lift small alien bug

parts.note: to up something is to lift or raise it

explanation.surface: Picking up a tiny insect from another planet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' looks like a creature beside 'alien'; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal synonym: to bug someone is to irritate them.

clue.text: Playwright that's unpleasant during address to queen?

indicators.note: 'during' means in the course of, so the first piece falls in the middle of the second

parts.note: Ma'am is how the Queen is addressed
ugh, a cry at something nasty

explanation.surface: A dramatist says something rude while speaking to the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The writer is better known for novels, which makes 'Playwright' less obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: W. Somerset Maugham had several hit plays in the 1920s, such as 'The Circle'.

clue.text: Game prince over how he addressed Mary de Bohun?

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'over' means above, so the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: Prince Hal, Shakespeare's young Henry V

parts.words: how he addressed Mary de Bohun?
parts.note: Mary de Bohun was his mother

explanation.surface: A historical question about how a royal prince spoke to a noblewoman.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary de Bohun, first wife of Henry IV, was Prince Hal's mother; the question mark admits the homely form of address is a guess.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a board game of jumping pieces, forerunner of Chinese chequers.

clue.text: Cried after snakes exposed to blast

indicators.note: 'after' means following, so this piece comes behind the next one

explanation.surface: Someone burst into tears after encountering snakes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snakes' looks like reptiles; it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a place laid open to strong gusts, 'blast' being a gust of wind.

clue.text: Small piece of land has a tenant

parts.note: a property with an occupant 'is' in the rented state; this pair of words becomes the verb
a place with a tenant has been rented out

explanation.surface: A small plot of land has somebody renting it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has a tenant' is read as 'is let', rented out, which spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a tiny island, a small piece of land in water.

clue.text: Unusual trace elements may do this

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters are out of their usual order

explanation.surface: A chemist notes that rare trace elements may behave in a particular way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trace elements' reads as one chemical phrase; 'trace' is the fodder and 'elements' starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: chemical elements combine and change in reactions.

clue.text: Who helps with setting leg and part of arm

parts.note: a leg of a journey is a stage
the hand is at the end of the arm

explanation.surface: A medic helps to set a broken leg and part of an arm.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is bone-setting; the setting is a theatre set.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a theatre worker who moves scenery and so helps with the set.
